title: Wrath (mēnis): the first word of the Iliad
greek: μῆνιν ἄειδε, θεά (mēnin aeide, thea)
short: The poem's first word is mēnis, a solemn, almost cosmic anger normally used of gods; its object, Akhilleus, is announced before the Muse is even addressed.
body: Murray keeps the Greek word order: 'The wrath sing, goddess'. Mēnis is not ordinary temper (cholos, kotos). In Homer it is used almost only of gods (Apollo at 1.75, Zeus, Poseidon) and of Akhilleus, and it denotes a lasting, sanctioned anger that answers a breach of the order of honour. Leonard Muellner argued that mēnis names a sanction against violations of the basic order of gods and men, so that Akhilleus' anger is placed on the level of divine retribution. The goddess addressed is the Muse, who knows the story and gives it to the singer (compare the fuller invocation at 2.484-93 and Od. 1.1). The proem names the theme, its cost ('countless woes'), and the moment where the song is to begin, the quarrel of Agamemnon and Akhilleus (1.6-7). The poem ends with the anger finally released in Book 24, so mēnis frames the whole work; Akhilleus himself renounces it at 19.67-75.

anchor: spoil for dogs and every bird
title: Spoil for dogs and birds: the unburied dead
greek: ἑλώρια … κύνεσσιν οἰωνοῖσί τε πᾶσι (helōria … kunessin oiōnoisi te pasi)
short: The worst fate for a Homeric warrior is to lie unburied and be eaten; the proem announces a theme that culminates in Akhilleus' treatment of Hector's corpse.
body: Line 4 opposes the 'souls' (psychai) sent to Hades with 'themselves' (autous), the bodies left as prey: as Leaf notes, for Homer the body is the real self and the psyche a mere shadow. The threat of exposure to dogs and birds recurs in boasts and threats throughout the poem (e.g. 2.393, 22.335-54) and reaches its climax when Akhilleus drags Hector and the gods intervene to preserve the body (24.18-21); Charles Segal traced this as a structuring theme. There is an ancient textual problem: Athenaeus reports that Zenodotus read daita, 'a feast for dogs and birds', instead of pasi, 'every' (bird). Leaf points out that Aeschylus (Suppliants 800-01) and Euripides (Ion 505, Hecuba 1077) seem to echo a 'feast' wording, and thought daita intrinsically better, though he kept the manuscript reading. Murray translates pasi.

title: The plan of Zeus (Dios boulē)
greek: Διὸς δ᾽ ἐτελείετο βουλή (Dios d' eteleieto boulē)
short: 'The will of Zeus was being accomplished': the narrator frames all the suffering as part of a divine design, whose content ancient and modern readers have disputed.
body: What is the 'plan' (boulē)? One ancient answer, preserved in the scholia, quotes the lost Cypria (fragment 1): Zeus planned the Trojan War itself to relieve the overburdened Earth of too many people. The other, favoured by Aristarchus and by most modern critics, reads it within the poem: Zeus's promise to Thetis at 1.508-30 to honour Akhilleus by letting the Achaeans be beaten, a plan announced at 2.3-4 ('how he might do honour to Achilles') and carried out through Books 8-18. Many readers think the phrase holds both: the local plan for Akhilleus serves a larger design of destruction. Leaf also discusses whether 'from the time when' in line 6 depends on the plan or on 'sing' in line 1 (the point where the song begins); he prefers the latter.

title: Apollo's plague and his descent 'like the night'
greek: νοῦσον … κακήν (noüson … kakēn) 1.10; λοιμός (loimos) 1.61; νυκτὶ ἐοικώς (nukti eoikōs) 1.47
short: The first event of the poem is a god's punishment: Apollo strides down from Olympus 'like the night' and shoots the camp with plague for nine days.
body: The narrator gives the cause briefly (1.9-12) and then dramatises it (1.43-52). Apollo comes down 'angered at heart', the arrows rattling on his shoulders, 'and his coming was like the night' (1.47): the first simile of the poem, short and ominous. He shoots first the mules and dogs, then the men, and 'the pyres of the dead burned thick'. The verb for his attack (epōikheto, 'visited') is used, Leaf observes, only of assaults made by a god or under divine inspiration. Zenodotus rejected lines 46-7 as spurious, but Leaf judged the couplet 'too fine to be sacrificed'. In Homer disease is a god's arrow; there is no natural explanation and the remedy is religious, which is why Akhilleus proposes asking a seer or priest (1.62-7). The plague also starts the quarrel, since its cure forces Agamemnon to give up Chryseis. Nine days followed by decisive action on the tenth is a recurrent Homeric rhythm (compare 6.174-5, 24.784-5).

title: Ransom (apoina)
greek: ἀπερείσι᾽ ἄποινα (apereisi' apoina)
short: Ransoming captives was an accepted institution; refusing a priest's ransom against the army's wish is Agamemnon's first offence.
body: Apoina is the price paid to recover a person, alive or dead. Captives taken in raids were regularly ransomed: Akhilleus had once sold or released Priam's son Lycaon (21.34-44) and Andromache's mother (6.425-7). So Chryses' request is normal and his gifts are 'past counting'. The whole army shouts assent (1.22-3) out of respect (aidōs) for the priest; Agamemnon alone refuses. The Iliad is framed by two ransom scenes: Book 1 opens with an old father refused, and Book 24 closes with an old father, Priam, whose ransom for Hector's body Akhilleus accepts. Critics such as C. W. Macleod have shown how deliberately the last book answers the first. Calchas' later demand that the girl be returned 'unbought, unransomed' (1.99) reverses the terms: the price of refusing ransom is to lose both girl and payment.

title: Chryses' wreaths and staff: the priest as suppliant
greek: στέμματ᾽ ἔχων … χρυσέῳ ἀνὰ σκήπτρῳ (stemmat' echōn … khruseōi ana skēptrōi)
short: The woollen fillets of Apollo wound on a golden staff mark Chryses as both priest and suppliant, under the god's protection.
body: The stemma is a band of wool. Leaf explains it as the token of suppliancy wrapped round the staff, like the wool-wreathed branch of suppliants in Aeschylus (Suppliants 23) and Virgil's 'Apollinis infula' (Aeneid 2.430); it is probably the priest's own fillet, or possibly the wreath from the god's image. By carrying the god's insignia, Chryses makes any insult to him an insult to Apollo, which is exactly how Agamemnon's threat ('lest your staff and the wreath of the god not protect you', 1.28) turns into a plague. The scene is the first of the poem's great supplications and ransom offers; it is balanced at the end of the poem when another old father, Priam, comes to the Achaean camp with ransom for his child and is received (Book 24).

title: Apollo 'who strikes from afar' (hekēbolos) and 'god of the silver bow'
greek: ἑκηβόλος (hekēbolos); ἑκάεργος (hekaergos); ἀργυρότοξος (argurotoxos)
short: Apollo's standing epithets present him as the archer whose arrows fall from a distance, bringing sudden death and disease.
body: Murray's 'who strikes from afar' renders hekēbolos, and 'who works from afar' (1.474, 479) renders hekaergos. The usual ancient derivation is from hekas, 'far off', with ballein, 'to throw, shoot'; the lexicon also records a possible link with hekōn, 'at will', which some scholars prefer. Either way the god is the archer, as 'god of the silver bow' (argurotoxos, 1.37) and the 'terrible twang of the silver bow' (1.49) remind us. In Homer, the arrows of Apollo (and of his sister Artemis) are the conventional cause of sudden death, sometimes a 'gentle' one (Od. 3.280, 15.410-11), and here of epidemic disease. The epithets therefore carry the plot: the priest prays to the archer, and the archer answers with plague.

title: Achaeans, Argives, Danaans: the Greeks of the Iliad
greek: ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοί (eüknēmides Akhaioi); Ἀργεῖοι (Argeioi); Δαναοί (Danaoi)
short: Homer never calls the Greek army 'Hellenes'; he uses three interchangeable names, Achaeans, Argives and Danaans, often with stock epithets such as 'well-greaved'.
body: 'Well-greaved' (eüknēmides) refers to the knēmides, shin-guards, a mark of the fully armed warrior; it is one of several fixed epithets of the Achaeans (with 'long-haired' and 'bronze-clad'), chosen largely for metrical convenience. The three collective names are used without difference of meaning. Thucydides (1.3) already noticed that Homer, though later than the war, never calls the whole army Hellenes: in the Catalogue (2.683-4) that name belongs only to Akhilleus' people in Phthiotis. Modern scholars have connected Achaioi with the Ahhiyawa of Hittite records and Danaoi with a people named in Egyptian texts, but these identifications remain debated. Murray varies the names as Homer does: Chryses addresses the 'well-greaved Achaeans' and then prays that the 'Danaans' may pay for his tears.

title: Chryse, Cilla and Tenedos
greek: Χρύσην … Κίλλαν τε ζαθέην Τενέδοιό τε (Khrusēn … Killan te zatheēn Tenedoio te)
short: Three cult places of Apollo near Troy: Chryse, Chryses' own town; Cilla; and the island of Tenedos (modern Bozcaada).
body: The prayer opens with the formal invocation of a god by the places where he is worshipped and which he 'stands over' (amphibebēkas) as protector. Tenedos is the island off the Troad (Bozcaada). Chryse and Cilla were small towns whose sites were already disputed in antiquity. Strabo (13.1.63) argued that Homer's Chryse lay on the Gulf of Adramyttium near Thebe, where the Achaeans had captured Chryseis (1.366-9), and that the later Chryse with the famous temple of Apollo Smintheus, near Hamaxitus on the west coast of the Troad (13.1.48), was a different place; others explained that Chryseis was merely visiting relatives at Thebe (both views are reported by Leaf). The geography also supports the narrative: Odysseus' embassy sails from the camp to Chryse, sacrifices, and returns the next day (1.430-87).

title: Smintheus (Sminthian Apollo), the mouse god
greek: Σμινθεῦ (Smintheu), from σμίνθος (sminthos), 'mouse'
short: Smintheus means 'mouse god': a cult title of Apollo in the Troad, probably linking him with mice as omens or carriers of plague, and with their destruction.
body: Ancient scholars derived the title from sminthos, said by the scholia to be the Cretan word for 'mouse'. Strabo (13.1.48) tells how Cretan settlers of the Troad were told by an oracle to stay where 'the earth-born' attacked them; at Hamaxitus field-mice gnawed their leather gear, so they settled and founded the cult of Apollo Smintheus. Aelian (On Animals 12.5) says tame mice were kept in the temple, and Leaf notes late coins of Alexandria Troas showing Apollo with a mouse at his feet. Interpretations differ. Leaf calls 'the common explanation' that he destroys the field-mice that ravage crops; others see the mouse as a symbol or carrier of plague, which Leaf grants is 'especially suitable here' and compares with the golden mice offered against plague in 1 Samuel 6:4-5. Andrew Lang proposed an old local mouse-cult absorbed by Apollo. So 'lord of mice' is accurate, and the plague link is a strong, widely held interpretation rather than a certainty. The Hellenistic temple of Apollo Smintheus survives at Gülpınar (Çanakkale).

title: 'Swift-footed Achilles': the noun-epithet formula
greek: πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς (podas ōkus Akhilleus)
short: The best-known Homeric formula: a fixed name-and-epithet unit that fills the end of the hexameter line, used whatever Akhilleus is doing.
body: Milman Parry showed that Homeric epithets form an economical system: for each hero there is usually one formula for each metrical slot, so that 'swift-footed Achilles' fits the second half of a line after a verb of speaking, while 'brilliant Achilles' (dios Akhilleus) and 'son of Peleus' fill other slots. The epithet thus belongs to the traditional diction of oral poetry and need not describe the moment: Akhilleus is 'swift-footed' while he sits motionless by his ships (1.488-9). Readers still feel the irony, since the fastest of heroes spends most of the poem idle and his speed matters at last in the pursuit of Hector (Book 22). Parry's findings, made with comparison to living South Slavic epic, transformed the study of Homer as oral-traditional poetry.

title: Calchas son of Thestor, best of bird-diviners
greek: Κάλχας Θεστορίδης οἰωνοπόλων ὄχ᾽ ἄριστος (Kalkhas Thestoridēs oiōnopolōn okh' aristos)
short: The army's seer, a reader of birds who knows 'the things that were, and that were to be, and that had been before', guided the fleet to Troy.
body: An oiōnopolos interprets the flight and cries of birds (oiōnoi), the commonest Homeric form of divination; Calchas' gift is said to come from Apollo. His knowledge of past, present and future (1.70) is the same formula Hesiod uses for what the Muses tell (Theogony 38), which links seer and poet. Calchas demands protection before speaking because he knows the truth will offend the king, and Agamemnon's answer, 'Prophet of evil' (1.106), suggests a history of unwelcome oracles. Many readers, ancient and modern, hear an allusion to Aulis, where in the wider tradition (the Cypria; Aeschylus, Agamemnon 184-247) Calchas required the sacrifice of Agamemnon's daughter Iphigeneia; the Iliad never mentions that story, so the allusion remains a possibility, not a fact. His interpretation of the portent at Aulis is recalled at 2.299-332.

title: Clytemnestra: Agamemnon's wife, and an ironic name
greek: Κλυταιμνήστρης προβέβουλα (Klutaimnēstrēs probeboula)
short: Agamemnon says he prefers the captive Chryseis to his wedded wife: an insult to Clytemnestra that later readers heard as grimly ironic.
body: This is the only time Clytemnestra is named in the Iliad, as Leaf notes (he adds that the better-attested spelling of the name is Klutaimēstrē). Agamemnon praises Chryseis as Clytemnestra's equal 'in form, stature, mind and handiwork', the standard qualities of a wife, and means to take her home to Argos. Audiences who knew the return story would think at once of its end: in the Odyssey (3.262-75, 11.405-34) Agamemnon is murdered on his homecoming by Aegisthus and Clytemnestra, and in Aeschylus' Agamemnon (458 BC) he brings another captive, Cassandra, home with him and both are killed. The Iliad does not say this, so the irony is created by the tradition around the poem, not stated in it. The line also shows Agamemnon treating women as property of status, which is exactly the logic of the quarrel over prizes.

title: Prize of honour (geras) and honour (timē)
greek: γέρας (geras); ἀγέραστος (agerastos); τιμή (timē)
short: A geras is the special share of spoil given to a leader as a public mark of standing; losing it means losing face, the real issue of the quarrel.
body: Agamemnon will not be 'without a prize' (agerastos, 1.119) because in this society honour (timē) is made visible in material things: the best spoils, the best portion at feasts, the first cup. Akhilleus replies that all booty has been shared out and cannot be taken back (1.123-6), and soon complains that Agamemnon always gets the larger prize though Akhilleus does most of the fighting (1.163-8). Briseis and Chryseis are therefore both persons and tokens of status, and the dispute is less about desire than about public recognition. As Leaf put it, 'the heroic point of honour is not abstract; it requires to be realized in the shape of ransom or material recompense.' Scholars of Homeric values (M. I. Finley; A. W. H. Adkins) used this scene to describe a 'shame culture' in which a man's worth depends on what others grant him; Akhilleus' later doubts about the whole system (9.315-43) begin here.

title: 'Dog-face': Akhilleus' insults
greek: κυνῶπα (kunōpa) 1.159; κυνὸς ὄμματ᾽ ἔχων, κραδίην δ᾽ ἐλάφοιο (kunos ommat' ekhōn, kradiēn d' elaphoio) 1.225
short: To call a man 'dog-eyed' or 'dog-faced' is to call him shameless; Akhilleus adds 'heart of a deer' to call Agamemnon a coward as well.
body: In Greek the dog stands for shamelessness: it eats anything and does not blush. Kunōps, 'dog-eyed', is used of Agamemnon here and by Helen of herself in self-reproach (3.180; compare 6.344). At 1.225 Akhilleus builds a full insult: 'heavy with wine, with the eyes of a dog but the heart of a deer' (Greek ommata, 'eyes'; Murray says 'face'), that is, brazen in grabbing but timid in battle, a man who never goes into ambush with the best. Other unheroic terms follow: 'people-devouring king' (dēmoboros, 1.231) and 'clothed in shamelessness' (1.149). Such open abuse of the supreme commander is extreme within the epic's code and shows how far the quarrel has gone. Later in Book 2 Thersites will repeat Akhilleus' charges and be beaten for it.

title: The Myrmidons, Akhilleus' people, and Phthia
greek: Μυρμιδόνες (Murmidones); Φθίη (Phthiē)
short: Akhilleus' followers from Phthia in southern Thessaly; ancient myth explained the name from murmēx, 'ant'.
body: Akhilleus' home is Phthia, 'deep-soiled, nurse of men' (1.155), in southern Thessaly, the kingdom of his father Peleus; in the Catalogue his people are called 'Myrmidons and Hellenes and Achaeans' (2.684). The name gave rise to a famous aetiological myth: when the island of Aegina was depopulated, Zeus turned ants (murmēkes) into people for Aeacus, Akhilleus' grandfather (Hesiod, fragment 205 Merkelbach-West; Strabo 8.6.16; Ovid, Metamorphoses 7.614-60). Strabo offers a rationalising version, that the early Aeginetans dug the soil like ants. The etymology is folk-etymology, but it was popular, and 'Myrmidon' came to mean in English a loyal follower who carries out orders without question. Agamemnon's taunt 'lord it over the Myrmidons' belittles Akhilleus as a merely local chief.

title: Briseis, and the captive women of the Iliad
greek: Βρισηΐδα καλλιπάρῃον (Brisēida kalliparēion)
short: Briseis, 'daughter of Briseus', Akhilleus' war-prize, taken from Lyrnessus; her seizure turns the quarrel into Akhilleus' withdrawal.
body: Both captive women are named only by patronymic: Chryseis is 'daughter of Chryses' and Briseis 'daughter of Briseus' (1.392). Later scholia supplied personal names (Astynome, Hippodameia). The origin of the name is uncertain: Leaf reports Fick's theory that it came from Bresa on Lesbos, where there was also a Chryse, so that in older legend both women were taken in a raid on Lesbos; but for Homer Briseis comes from Lyrnessus. Akhilleus took Briseis when he sacked Lyrnessus and killed her husband and brothers (2.688-93; 19.291-6); Chryseis was taken in the raid on Thebe, 'the sacred city of Eetion' (1.366-9), the father of Hector's wife Andromache, whose family Akhilleus destroyed there (6.414-28). Briseis 'went unwilling' (1.348), and in her one speech, her lament over Patroclus (19.282-300), she tells her own story and remembers Patroclus' kindness. Recent criticism and fiction (for example Pat Barker, The Silence of the Girls, 2018) have made her silence in Book 1 a starting point for reading the poem from the captives' side.

title: Athena stops Akhilleus' sword
greek: ἦλθε δ᾽ Ἀθήνη οὐρανόθεν (ēlthe d' Athēnē ouranothen); ξανθῆς δὲ κόμης ἕλε (xanthēs de komēs hele)
short: As Akhilleus half-draws his sword, Athena, visible to him alone, seizes him by the hair and persuades him to fight with words instead.
body: The scene is the classic example of Homeric 'double motivation': Akhilleus is already weighing two courses (1.188-92), and the goddess appears at the moment of choice, so the decision is both his and the god's. E. R. Dodds called such moments 'psychic intervention'; Albin Lesky showed that divine and human causes run side by side rather than excluding each other. The details are physical and vivid: she stands behind him, grabs his fair hair, and her eyes 'shone terribly' (1.200); only he sees her (1.198). Athena is sent by Hera, who cares for both kings (1.195-6), and she promises 'three times as many glorious gifts' in future (1.213-14), a promise fulfilled by Agamemnon's offer in Book 9 and the gifts of Book 19. Akhilleus obeys, but turns at once to violent words.

title: 'Winged words' (epea pteroenta)
greek: ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα (epea pteroenta prosēuda)
short: One of Homer's most frequent speech-introductions: words that fly from the speaker to the hearer, like birds or feathered arrows.
body: The whole line 'and he spoke to her winged words' is a fixed formula, used scores of times in the Iliad and Odyssey to introduce speech. Its exact force is debated. Some take the image from birds (words that fly swiftly and surely to their target); others from the feathered arrow, since pteroeis is used of arrows; others think it marks speech that is emotionally charged or that goes straight to the addressee. Because it is formulaic, it rarely carries special emphasis, but here it introduces Akhilleus' first words to a goddess at a moment of high tension. Compare the opposite image of 'unwinged' (apteros) speech in the Odyssey (e.g. 17.57), where a word remains silently with the hearer.

title: 'Aegis-bearing Zeus' (aigiokhos)
greek: αἰγιόχοιο Διὸς τέκος (aigiokhoio Dios tekos)
short: Zeus's epithet aigiokhos means 'holding the aegis', the terrifying goatskin-like shield or cloak that he and Athena shake to rout armies.
body: Aigiokhos combines aigis with the root of ekhein, 'to hold'. The aegis (literally connected with aix, 'goat', and perhaps with kataigis, 'squall') is a divine object: made by Hephaestus for Zeus (15.308-10), it is fringed with tassels (2.447-9), bears the Gorgon's head (5.738-42), and when shaken it brings thunder and panic (4.166-8, 17.593-6). Apollo and Athena borrow it. Whether it was imagined as a goatskin cape or as a shield is disputed. Leaf took it as a symbol of the storm-cloud and, following Reichel, as a primitive shield of hairy hide, which survived as divine armour; later art shows Athena wearing it as a cape fringed with snakes, with the Gorgon's head. Akhilleus' address to Athena as 'daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus' is a formula, but it reminds him that his visitor carries her father's authority. The object itself is described in Book 2.

title: 'Bright-eyed' (glaukōpis) Athena
greek: θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη (thea glaukōpis Athēnē)
short: Athena's standing epithet glaukōpis means 'with gleaming (or grey) eyes'; an old alternative interpretation is 'owl-faced', from glaux, 'owl'.
body: Glaukos describes the gleaming, pale blue-grey of the sea or of olive leaves, and glaukōpis is normally understood as 'with flashing, bright, or grey eyes'; Murray uses both 'bright-eyed' and 'flashing-eyed' (2.166). Because the owl (glaux) was Athena's bird at Athens, some nineteenth-century scholars, notably Heinrich Schliemann, argued that the word originally meant 'owl-faced' and preserved an animal form of the goddess, just as boōpis Hera ('ox-eyed') might once have been 'cow-faced'. Most modern scholars think the epithet describes the eyes, and in this very scene her eyes 'shone terribly' (1.200). Murray's 'bright-eyed' also renders a different word, helikōpis ('quick-glancing' or 'with curving eyes'), used of Chryseis at 1.98; the English obscures the distinction.

title: Akhilleus' oath by the sceptre
greek: ναὶ μὰ τόδε σκῆπτρον (nai ma tode skēptron)
short: Akhilleus swears by the speaker's staff, the sceptre held by judges, that the Achaeans will long for him, then hurls it to the ground.
body: The staff is not Akhilleus' own: as Leaf explains, it is the skēptron handed by a herald to whoever has the floor in the assembly (compare 23.567-8; Od. 2.37-8), and it is carried by 'those who guard the ordinances (themistes) that come from Zeus' (1.238-9). Akhilleus makes it the guarantee of his oath and describes it with bitter precision: cut from its stump in the mountains, stripped of bark by bronze, it will never grow leaves again. Many readers take the dead wood as an image of the irrevocable break between him and the community, and as a contrast with Agamemnon's sceptre, which has a divine pedigree (2.100-8). Throwing it down, 'studded with golden nails', is a gesture of rejection of the whole order it represents. The prophecy, 'a longing for Achilles will come upon the sons of the Achaeans', governs the next sixteen books. Virgil imitates the oath in Latinus' oath by his sceptre (Aeneid 12.206-11).

title: 'Man-slaying Hector': Hector's first appearance
greek: ὑφ᾽ Ἕκτορος ἀνδροφόνοιο (huph' Hektoros androphonoio)
short: Hector is first named in Akhilleus' oath, with the epithet androphonos, 'man-slaying', which will later describe Akhilleus' own hands.
body: Androphonos, 'man-killing', is Hector's usual epithet in this metrical position and marks him as the Trojans' chief warrior; his name is often connected with ekhein, 'to hold', as the one who 'holds' or protects the city. It is telling that he enters the poem in Akhilleus' mouth, as the man who will kill the Achaeans once Akhilleus withdraws, so the two are linked from the beginning. The same adjective returns at the poem's most moving moment: Priam kisses 'the terrible, man-slaying hands' of Akhilleus, which had killed many of his sons (24.478-9). Hector leads the Trojan forces at the end of Book 2 (2.807-18) but first speaks in Book 3 (3.39-57); his scenes inside Troy in Book 6 show the family his fighting protects.

title: Nestor of Pylos, the old counsellor
greek: Νέστωρ ἡδυεπὴς … λιγὺς Πυλίων ἀγορητής (Nestōr hēduepēs … ligus Puliōn agorētēs)
short: The oldest of the Achaean kings, honey-tongued, ruling over a third generation; he tries to reconcile the quarrel with an example from his youth.
body: Nestor is introduced with a cluster of terms for persuasive speech: 'sweet of speech', 'clear-voiced orator', with words 'sweeter than honey'. Two generations have passed in his lifetime (1.250-2), so he speaks with the authority of the past. His typical method, seen here for the first time, is the paradigm: an example from his youth, when he fought beside far greater men (Peirithous, Caeneus, Theseus) against the 'mountain-dwelling centaurs', and they listened to him; the moral is that younger, lesser men should listen too. Homer calls the centaurs phēres, 'wild beasts', and never says they were half-horse. The line naming Theseus (1.265) recurs in the Hesiodic Shield of Heracles (182); Leaf notes that Theseus appears elsewhere in Homer only in doubtful Odyssey passages, one of which an ancient writer (cited by Plutarch, Theseus 20) called an interpolation by Peisistratus to please the Athenians, so this line too may be an Athenian addition. Nestor's speeches grow longer through the poem (7.124-60, 11.656-803) and are sometimes read as affectionately comic. Here, notably, his advice fails: both kings agree he has 'spoken as is right' and do nothing different. His home, Pylos, has been identified with the Mycenaean 'Palace of Nestor' at Ano Englianos in Messenia, excavated by Carl Blegen from 1939.

title: Patroclus, son of Menoetius
greek: Μενοιτιάδῃ (Menoitiadēi)
short: Patroclus enters the poem silently by his patronymic; Akhilleus' closest companion, his death in Book 16 will bring Akhilleus back to battle.
body: He is first 'the son of Menoetius' (1.307), introduced, as Leaf remarks, by his patronymic alone, as if the audience already knew the story; he is named at 1.337, where he obeys Akhilleus and hands over Briseis without a word. His background appears later: as a boy he killed a playmate by accident and was received by Peleus and brought up with Akhilleus (23.84-90); his father Menoetius told him to advise the younger but stronger Akhilleus (11.785-9). His gentleness is stressed by Briseis (19.295-300). The Iliad presents the two as inseparable companions (hetairoi) and does not describe them as lovers; that reading appears in classical Athens (Aeschylus' lost Myrmidons; Plato, Symposium 180a, where Phaedrus discusses which was lover and which beloved). The quiet entrance is typical of Homeric technique: the figure on whom the plot will turn is introduced without emphasis.

title: The 'wine-dark' sea (oinops pontos)
greek: οἴνοπα πόντον (oinopa ponton)
short: Homer's famous colour-word for the sea, literally 'wine-faced'; its sense, and even its presence in this line, are debated.
body: Oinops means 'wine-looking', and is also used of oxen (13.703), so it may refer less to hue than to a dark, shining or glinting quality, as of red wine in a cup. In the nineteenth century W. E. Gladstone used such phrases to argue that the Greeks had an undeveloped colour sense; modern scholars prefer to say that Greek colour terms stress brightness, darkness and movement more than hue. In this particular line there is a textual choice: the manuscripts read oinopa ponton, but Aristarchus read apeirona ponton, 'the boundless sea', perhaps because 'wine-dark' seemed to clash with the 'grey' (polios) sea earlier in the line. Murray follows the manuscripts' oinopa. Leaf defends oinopa, seeing a vivid contrast between the purple deep water and the greenish-grey shallows by the shore. Akhilleus goes apart and looks out over the sea before praying to his mother, a sea-goddess: the setting prepares her appearance 'like a mist' from the grey water.

anchor: so brief a span of life
title: Akhilleus' short life (minunthadios)
greek: μινυνθάδιόν περ ἐόντα (minunthadion per eonta); ὠκύμορος (ōkumoros) 1.417
short: From the first book Akhilleus knows he will die young; because his life is short, he says, Zeus owes him honour.
body: Akhilleus' prayer joins two ideas, as Leaf notes: 'you bore me, a man of brief span', and 'since my life is short, it should at least be glorious'. Thetis confirms it, calling him 'doomed to a speedy death' (ōkumoros, 1.417) and 'laden with sorrow above all men'. The theme becomes explicit in Book 9, where Akhilleus reveals his choice between two fates, a long life without fame at home or death at Troy with 'imperishable fame' (kleos aphthiton, 9.410-16), and decisive in Book 18, when he chooses to avenge Patroclus knowing his own death will follow Hector's (18.95-6). This awareness of mortality is what gives Akhilleus' anger its depth: honour is the only compensation for death. Laura Slatkin argued that the poem's emphasis on Thetis' grief keeps that mortality constantly before us.

title: Briareus-Aegaeon and the plot to bind Zeus
greek: ἑκατόγχειρον … ὃν Βριάρεων καλέουσι θεοί, ἄνδρες δέ τε πάντες Αἰγαίων᾽ (hekatonkheiron … hon Briareōn kaleousi theoi, andres de te pantes Aigaiōn')
short: Akhilleus recalls how Thetis once saved Zeus from a revolt of Hera, Poseidon and Athena by summoning the hundred-handed giant Briareus.
body: The story is not found elsewhere, and its gods are significant: Hera, Poseidon and Athena are exactly the gods who favour the Achaeans in the Iliad. Briareus is one of the Hundred-Handers who in Hesiod help Zeus defeat the Titans (Theogony 147-53, 617-735). The phrase 'whom the gods call Briareus, but all men Aegaeon' is the first instance of Homer's 'language of the gods', in which gods and mortals use different names for the same thing (compare Batieia, 2.813-14; Xanthus/Scamander, 20.74). 'Mightier than his father' refers to Poseidon, Briareus' father in the legend, who was himself sometimes called Aegaeon (Leaf). Zenodotus rejected 1.396-406 as superfluous; Leaf replies that the passage exists to inform the audience, and discusses whether the 'divine' names are archaic survivals. Scholars disagree about the episode's status: M. M. Willcock argued that Homer freely invents such mythical precedents to suit the speaker's purpose, while Laura Slatkin read it as a trace of an old tradition of Thetis' cosmic power over Zeus.

title: Supplication (hiketeia): clasping the knees
greek: λάβε γούνων … ὑπ᾽ ἀνθερεῶνος ἑλοῦσα (labe gounōn … hup' anthereōnos helousa)
short: To clasp a person's knees and touch his chin is the formal gesture of supplication, which places the suppliant under the protection of Zeus.
body: Akhilleus tells his mother to 'clasp his knees' (1.407), and at 1.500-2 Thetis does exactly that, with her left hand on Zeus's knees and her right under his chin. John Gould's classic study showed that such physical contact creates a ritual claim that is hard to refuse; Zeus, the god of suppliants, is here himself the one supplicated. When Zeus is silent, Thetis 'held to him, clinging close' and asks again (1.512-13), forcing an answer. Leaf suggests the gesture may derive from the last resort of a disarmed warrior, who clasps his enemy's legs to hamper him and pushes aside his face so that he cannot aim the final blow until the plea has been heard. Supplication structures the poem: Chryses supplicates the Achaeans (1.15), Phoenix tells of Meleager's suppliants (9.574-96), Lycaon supplicates Akhilleus in vain (21.64-119), and Priam kneels and kisses Akhilleus' hands (24.477-9), the climactic supplication of the poem, and one that succeeds.

title: Sacrifice and feast: a Homeric type-scene
greek: οὐλοχύτας (oulokhutas) 1.449; ἑκατόμβη (hekatombē); δαιτὸς ἐΐσης (daitos eïsēs) 1.468; παιήων (paiēōn) 1.473
short: The sacrifice at Chryse follows a fixed sequence of ritual acts, repeated almost word for word in Book 2: the fullest description of Greek animal sacrifice in Homer.
body: The steps are: washing hands and taking up barley grains (merely bruised, Leaf suggests, a ritual relic of a time before grinding); prayer; sprinkling the grains; drawing back the victims' heads, cutting the throats and flaying; cutting out the thigh-bones, wrapping them in a double layer of fat with raw pieces on top, and burning them for the god with a libation of wine; tasting the entrails (splankhna); roasting and eating the rest at an 'equal feast' (dais eïsē), where everyone shares alike; then wine and song. A hecatomb, nominally 'a hundred oxen', here means a great sacrifice of bulls and goats. Hesiod explains why gods receive the bones and fat (Theogony 535-57, Prometheus' trick). The youths then appease Apollo all day with the paean (paiēōn), a song of rejoicing and propitiation; Leaf notes it need not be addressed to Apollo (the Achaeans sing one over Hector's death, 22.391), though the name is linked with Paiēon, the healer of the gods (5.401). Compare the sacrifice at Pylos, Od. 3.430-63. Walter Burkert's studies remain the standard account of this ritual.

title: 'Rosy-fingered Dawn' (rhododaktulos Ēōs)
greek: ἦμος δ᾽ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς (ēmos d' ērigeneia phanē rhododaktulos Ēōs)
short: The first occurrence of Homer's most famous formula: a whole line marking a new day, in which Dawn's 'fingers' are the rosy rays of light spreading over the sky.
body: Literally: 'and when early-born (ērigeneia) rosy-fingered Dawn appeared'. The line is a full-verse formula that marks the passage of time; it is far commoner in the Odyssey than in the Iliad. Dawn (Ēōs) is a goddess, and the image of 'fingers' is usually taken to refer to the streaks of light that stretch across the eastern sky before sunrise. Sappho borrowed the epithet for the moon, 'rosy-fingered' after sunset (fragment 96), one of the earliest examples of a Homeric formula reused with new meaning. Here it closes the sacrifice scene at Chryse and opens the voyage back, with a favouring wind from Apollo, the sail 'belly' filled and the 'dark wave' singing at the stem (1.481-2).

title: The nod of Zeus
greek: ἦ καὶ κυανέῃσιν ἐπ᾽ ὀφρύσι νεῦσε Κρονίων (ē kai kuaneēisin ep' ophrusi neuse Kroniōn)
short: Zeus's nod is his irrevocable promise; three lines describing it inspired Pheidias' gold-and-ivory statue of Zeus at Olympia.
body: Zeus explains that a nod is 'the surest token among the immortals': what he nods to cannot be recalled, false or unfulfilled (1.525-7). The poet then shows it: the dark brows bend, the ambrosial hair sways, and great Olympus shakes. Strabo (8.3.30) reports that the sculptor Pheidias, asked what model he had followed for his statue of Zeus at Olympia (one of the Seven Wonders), quoted these lines. Virgil imitated them for Jupiter ('adnuit, et totum nutu tremefecit Olympum', Aeneid 9.106, 10.115). The scene seals the 'plan of Zeus' announced in the proem: from this nod come the Achaean defeats of the following books. It also launches the comic quarrel on Olympus, since Hera saw Thetis at Zeus's knees.

title: 'Silver-footed Thetis', daughter of the old man of the sea
greek: ἀργυρόπεζα Θέτις θυγάτηρ ἁλίοιο γέροντος (arguropeza Thetis thugatēr halioio gerontos)
short: Akhilleus' mother is a sea-goddess, daughter of the 'old man of the sea' (Nereus); her standing epithet means 'silver-footed'.
body: Arguropeza probably evokes the gleam of a sea-nymph's feet in the water. Thetis lives in the depths 'beside the old man, her father' (1.358), the sea-god whom later poets name Nereus; Leaf notes that Homer never names him, and names the Nereids only in a passage of doubtful authenticity (18.38-52). In the wider myth Zeus and Poseidon both courted her until it was prophesied that her son would be greater than his father, and she was married instead to the mortal Peleus (Pindar, Isthmian 8.26-47). The Iliad never tells this story directly, but Laura Slatkin argued that it lies behind Thetis' unusual power over Zeus: by not fathering Akhilleus, Zeus kept his throne, and Thetis' claim on him (1.503-4) carries that history. In the Iliad she is above all the grieving mother who rises 'like a mist' from the sea (1.359), comforts her son and pleads for him, as she will again in Book 18 and Book 24.

title: 'Ox-eyed' and 'white-armed' Hera
greek: βοῶπις πότνια Ἥρη (boōpis potnia Hērē); λευκώλενος Ἥρη (leukōlenos Hērē)
short: Hera's two standing epithets: boōpis, 'ox-eyed' (large, dark-eyed), and leukōlenos, 'white-armed' (pale-skinned, a mark of feminine beauty).
body: Boōpis is applied to Hera and to some mortal women (e.g. Clymene, 3.144), so in Homer it is a term of beauty: large, lustrous eyes like a cow's. Nineteenth-century scholars proposed that it preserved an earlier cow-form of the goddess, as glaukōpis was said to mean an owl-faced Athena; few now accept this. Potnia means 'lady, mistress', an old title already found in Mycenaean Linear B tablets. Leukōlenos, 'white-armed', reflects the ideal of pale skin for women who stay indoors, as against the sun-darkened skin of men; it is first used at 1.55, where Hera prompts Akhilleus to call the assembly. Her actions in Book 1 show her character: she sends Athena to stop Akhilleus, watches Zeus closely, and reproaches him for secret plans, until his threat of force silences her (1.565-9).

title: Hephaestus' fall to Lemnos and the gods' laughter
greek: Σίντιες ἄνδρες (Sinties andres) 1.594; ἄσβεστος … γέλως (asbestos … gelōs) 1.599
short: Hephaestus calms Hera by recalling how Zeus once hurled him from heaven to Lemnos, then hobbles about pouring wine and sets the gods laughing.
body: Lemnos was sacred to Hephaestus (its city was later called Hephaestia); Leaf connects this with the 'Lemnian Fire' on Mount Mosychlus, probably a natural gas jet rather than a volcano. The Sintians were early inhabitants of the island (Od. 8.294 calls them 'of savage speech'), perhaps related to the Sintoi, a Thracian tribe named by Thucydides (2.98.1). The Iliad gives a second, different account of his fall at 18.394-9 (Leaf), where Hera throws him out because he was born lame and Thetis rescues him; the inconsistency shows how freely Homer adapts myth to the speaker. The scene ends Book 1 in deliberate contrast with its opening. Among men, a quarrel over a prize leads to death; among the gods, a quarrel over mortals dissolves into 'unquenchable laughter' (asbestos gelōs) at the lame smith bustling about as wine-pourer, a role usually given to graceful youths. Leaf notes that the phrase 'Homeric laughter' comes from this line. Critics such as Jasper Griffin have stressed this contrast: divine life is without lasting consequence, which makes human suffering more serious.
